title: Hindu Temples: What Happened to Them, Vol. 1
byline: by Arun Shourie, Harsh Narain, Jay Dubashi, Ram Swarup and Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · 1990 · subtitled A Preliminary Survey
lede: Published at the height of the Ayodhya dispute, this volume makes one argument from several angles: that building mosques on demolished temples was a pattern, not an exception. It opens with Arun Shourie's discovery of a book by a rector of the Nadwatul Ulama in Lucknow that names such mosques, Babri among them. It closes with Goel's list of Muslim monuments across India said to stand on temple sites or to reuse temple materials. Koenraad Elst later called it the most important book of the controversy.

note: The list is, in the authors' words, “a preliminary survey” compiled largely from older archaeological reports and gazetteers. They acknowledge it may contain errors, and many entries rest on local tradition rather than excavation. This page counts and summarises the list. It does not verify individual entries.

sections.title: The list, counted by state
sections.lede: Each entry names a mosque, dargah, idgah or fort and marks it as standing on a temple site, built from temple materials, or a converted temple. Counts follow the book's state headings, which predate several later state reorganisations.
sections.note: We counted entries tagged “temple site”, “temple materials used” or “converted temple” in the online text: 1,492 in all (1,138 site, 334 materials, 20 converted). Delhi's list, written as one paragraph per area from Mehrauli onwards, is not included in the count.

sections.title: A Muslim scholar's own list
sections.lede: Shourie found that Maulana Hakim Sayid Abdul Hai, a rector of the Nadwatul Ulama and father of its later head Ali Mian, had written a chapter on “The Mosques of Hindustan”. He found the English edition hard to get. Abdul Hai names these, among others:
